To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) for the mutual exclusion problem, there exists a fast algorithm that is correct in the absence of process failures, (ii) for the consensus problem, there exists an algorithm that is correct even in the presence of process failures, and (iii) both of these algorithms are fast, i.e., they have constant time complexity in the presence of failures, in the absence or presence of contention.

(1) for mutual exclusion, a process needs to delay itself for at most 4 ⨀ Δ time units in the presence of contentions; and (2) for consensus, a process needs delay itself for at at most 1 ⨀ Δ time units in the worst-case scenario.

(i) for mutual exclusion, there exists a solution that has constant worst-case time complexity in the presence of arbitrary contention; and (ii) for consensus, there exists a deterministic solution that is optimal in the presence of one or more Byzantine processes, and there also exists a deterministic solution with constant worst-case time that is optimal in absence of contention.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (1) Can we construct fast algorithms for mutual exclusion and consensus in concurrent systems in which the memory access time has a known upper bound? (2) What is the time complexity of these algorithms?
fast algorithms for mutual exclusion and consensus in systems where memory access time is known and bounded.
fast timing-based algorithms for mutual exclusion and consensus in concurrent systems with a known upper bound on memory access times, and we show that these problems can be solved in constant time.

, in the absence or in the presence of (adversarial) contention, the time complexity of the presented mutual exclusion and consensus algorithms is constant.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
for any given number of processes, we can design fast algorithms for mutual exclusion and consensus that are optimal in the sense that no faster solution is possible.
we have presented fast timing-based algorithms for both mutual exclusion and consensus.
the time complexity of our solutions is constant, and the delay is bounded by the access time of the shared memory.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the absence and presence of contention, fast timing-based algorithms can be designed that have constant time complexity, i.e. independent of the number of processes, and the upper bound on memory access times.

, in concurrent systems where the memory access time is known, fast solutions to the synchronization problem can be obtained by using only a few accesses to the shared data structure, which is the main difference between our solutions and the ones that are known in the literature for concurrent systems where the upper bound on memory access time is not known.
fast timing-based algorithms can be designed for concurrent systems with bounded memory access time.
